item.title: SALES: Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no new build can quite replicate. From sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?). Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

item.title: REVIEW: Malwarebytes Free Review: A Free Removal Tool for Most Malware
item.description:
Source: PCMag
A PC without antivirus protection is just waiting to be infected with malware. When it does, you naturally rush to install that missing protection. Sometimes, though, the malware hooks into the system so thoroughly that it blocks that installation. Other times, you’ve done your best, but the malware slips past your antivirus. Malwarebytes Free aims to rescue you from those situations when a regular antivirus fails, and it does a solid job. With no real-time protection, however, it’s not intended as your only defense. You should use it alongside a full-powered free antivirus like Avast One Free or AVG AntiVirus Free, our Editors’ Choice winners. After the quick and simple installation of the main antivirus app, the installer offers to add Browser Guard to your default browser. Don’t turn down this offer—Browser Guard does a lot for you, as you’ll see below. If you use more than one browser, you’ll want to install it in all of them. Well, Chrome, Edge, and Firefox anyway. Note that anybody can download Browser Guard and use it independently of the antivirus reviewed here. This app’s main window features a simple menu on the left with five main items at the top: Dashboard, Privacy, Identity, Tools, and Scam Guard. At the bottom of the menu, you’ll find icons for Account and Settings. On the right, a large panel houses the Malwarebytes Trusted Advisor feature. Much like the AutoPilot feature in Bitdefender Antivirus Free, Trusted Advisor reports your protection status, showing a score from 0% to 100% and a link to advice on boosting it. Everybody wants a top score, right? In the middle are three wide panels titled Scanner, Detection History, and Real-Time Protection, with a bigger panel below devoted to VPN protection. In this free edition, the Real-Time Protection component is disabled. Previously, the VPN panel was also disabled, but now it offers free access limited to 10GB per month. For comparison, Avast’s 5GB per week translates to about 22GB per month, double what you get for free with Malwarebytes. But other competitors offer less, or much less. Bitdefender offers 200 MB of bandwidth per day on its free VPN tier, which is a bit over 6GB per month. With Tunnel Bear, you can use 2GB of VPN bandwidth per month. And Avira Free Security grants a stingy 0.5GB per month. Simple-minded signature-based malware detection alone isn't enough in the modern world of zero-day attacks and polymorphic malware. Every successful antivirus adds heuristic and behavior-based detection, as well as other non-signature protection layers. In Malwarebytes Premium Security, machine learning and detection of anomalous behavior catch many malware samples. Exploit protection watches attack vectors and heads off exploits. The Premium edition's anti-ransomware engine relies solely on behavioral detection. At one time, Malwarebytes took the position that normal testing procedures simply weren’t appropriate for the company’s emphasis on active, prevalent threats and advanced detection methods. Currently, though, the company is working with all five labs, aiming to achieve good scores and perhaps improve the testing process. Poland-based AVLab Cybersecurity Foundation is the latest addition to the collection of labs I track. This lab rates apps based on the percentage of malware samples they detect. Half of the tested products, including Malwarebytes, reached 100% in this lab’s latest test. None of the rest scored lower than 99.52%. With MRG-Effitas, apps don’t get a numeric score. If they prevent every malware attack during testing, they pass at Level 1. An app that initially misses one or more samples but resolves the issue within 24 hours passes Level 2. Anything else is a failure. Malwarebytes and Avast are the only apps to take Level 1 certification in the latest round of testing. Based in London, SE Labs takes a somewhat unusual approach to testing. This lab’s researchers use a capture-and-replay system to expose every antivirus tested to precisely the same real-world attack. Apps can receive certification at five possible levels: AAA, AA, A, B, and C. In the latest iteration of this test, Malwarebytes, TotalAV Free Edition, and Webroot Essentials achieved AA certification, while the rest achieved AAA certification. Experts at AV-Test Institute rate antivirus apps on protection, performance, and usability. That last category means the app avoids false positives, which are valid programs mistakenly tagged as malware. An antivirus can receive up to six points in each category, for a maximum of 18 points. Malwarebytes, along with almost all tested apps, reached a perfect 18 in this lab’s latest test. AV-Comparatives regularly publishes more than a dozen tests. Of those, I track two malware detection tests and one that measures performance impact. An app that passes receives Standard certification, while those that don’t make the cut get the label Tested. Those going beyond merely passing can earn Advanced or Advanced+ certification. In the latest of these tests, Malwarebytes reached Advanced for performance, but scored one Standard and one Tested in the other two. Bitdefender is the only antivirus app currently holding Advanced+ in all three tests. My lab score algorithm maps results from each of the five labs onto a 10-point scale. The fact that all five labs include Malwarebytes in their latest results is impressive. It means that all five considered the app important enough to cover, and that Malwarebytes was willing to pay the testing fees. Malwarebytes received several perfect scores, but it did fail one test. Its aggregate score of 8.7 reflects these mixed scores. Avast and Norton AntiVirus Plus are the only other apps currently covered by all five labs, and they both managed an impressive aggregate score of 9.7 points. Remember, though, that even if Malwarebytes Premium earned top scores from many labs, those scores wouldn’t directly apply to this review because they evaluate an antivirus tool’s ability to defend against malware attacks using real-time protection. You call on Malwarebytes Free for those occasions when your real-time antivirus failed to defend you, perhaps because you forgot to renew it. Malwarebytes Free does not offer any real-time protection. With the rise of ransomware attacks on businesses, governments, and individuals, ransomware protection is more important than ever. However, ransomware is intrinsically different from other kinds of malware. Most types of malware want to use your computer's resources, whether for mining bitcoins, launching DDoS attacks, or stealing your personal data. Typically, they aim to avoid notice, which means they carefully avoid any visible harm to the computer. A post-infestation antivirus cleanup can scour your computer's crannies and crevices for malware, restoring it to a safe, secure state. Ransomware, on the other hand, only stays quiet until it has done its nefarious work, locking away your important files in an unreadable, encrypted form. Once finished, it displays its ransom terms. Removing the ransomware at this point doesn't help. It could even interfere with your ability to get your files decrypted, should you decide to pay the ransom. Malwarebytes Premium eliminates ransomware before it attacks. Like other cleanup-only antivirus tools, Malwarebytes Free can't do anything once your files have already been encrypted into gibberish. Usually, I test malware protection by challenging an antivirus utility to prevent the installation of my malware sample collection. However, as noted, Malwarebytes Free doesn't include real-time protection. With no help from the labs, I had to find some way to evaluate its virus-busting skills. So, skipping the ransomware, I launched my samples in groups of five, allowed them some time to finish installing, and challenged Malwarebytes to clean up each mess. The time required for these scans ranged from about 1 to 4 minutes, with an average of 2.75 minutes. At the end of each scan, Malwarebytes displayed its findings. By carefully examining those reports, I determined which samples it detected. Given the number of traces found, the app suggested running a deep scan for several groups. The deep scan times averaged just under an hour, while the current average scan time is just under two hours. Yes, this app’s initial scan remains blazingly fast, but if it finds signs of malware, it’s worth your while to let it take as long as it needs to root out the traces. Like Sophos Home Premium, Malwarebytes detected 99% of my current samples. Had Malwarebytes perfectly removed every trace of the malware it detected, it would have scored 9.9 points. However, the scans left behind numerous traces of malware, including executable programs and data files. Leaving behind executable programs halves a sample's score, while leaving behind large amounts of data files shaves off additional points from the score. Overall, Malwarebytes scored 8.2 points, much better than its previous test score of 6.7. Once again, though, Malwarebytes does not attempt to block malware in its free edition. As a cleanup-only tool, Malwarebytes can be forgiven for eliminating the essential, active malware files, leaving the rest to be swept away by your regular antivirus. For a different sort of test, I rolled back the virtual machine testbed to a snapshot before any malware samples were launched and ran a full scan. Malwarebytes detected and quarantined 100% of the samples, including all ransomware samples. It also eliminated 99% of my hand-modified samples, an unusually high detection rate for them. If you’re lucky enough to run a scan between the time ransomware enters your system and the time it springs into action, the free scan could help, at least in theory. Since my last review, Malwarebytes has made an effort to keep your PC malware-free by scheduling a monthly scan. This doesn’t do any good in an emergency, but it might serve to eliminate threats, even ransomware threats, before they can launch. When you install Malwarebytes, whether Free or Premium, the app prompts you to add the Browser Guard extension for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. If you skip this step at installation, you can download the extension later. Browser Guard aims to protect against malware-hosting URLs, ads and trackers, tech support scams, sites with bad reputations, and more. I put those aims to the test. As far as ad-blocking goes, it seems to do the job. I installed Browser Guard in Chrome and then visited several ad-laden sites in both Chrome and an unprotected browser. The extension visibly removed ads. By clicking its toolbar icon, I could view specifics about ads and trackers on the current site or check statistics of past activity. The list of trackers is interactive—if you trust any of the tracking sites, you can click on them so Malwarebytes will stop blocking them. I doubt many will take advantage of this fine-tuning, though. My malicious URL blocking test uses a feed supplied by London-based testing lab MRG-Effitas, consisting of malware-hosting URLs discovered in the last few days. Most antivirus tools get two chances to fend off a malware download. First, they can divert the browser away from the malware-hosting URL. Second, they can use real-time protection to eliminate the malware payload. With no real-time protection, Browser Guard only gets one swing at each malware-hosting URL. I found that when Browser Guard blocked dangerous pages, it explained why, stating that the page contained a Trojan, riskware, or suspicious content, for example. However, after that initial screening, it couldn’t actively check the downloaded file for malware. With this limited detection, Browser Guard still fended off just 92% of the malware-hosting pages. That’s quite a bit better than its previous scores, which came in around 75% Even so, other antivirus apps have done significantly better. Avira, McAfee+, and Panda Free Antivirus all scored 100% in their latest malicious URL blocking tests. Emsisoft Anti-Malware, Sophos, and UltraAV reached 99%. In the earlier malware removal test, I noticed that Malwarebytes did a better job of recognizing and eliminating malware installers and startup files than of removing active malware. Just to see what would happen, I ran a scan on the Downloads folder. That scan detected and quarantined all but two of the verified malware payloads. On-demand scanning isn’t normally part of this test, but Malwarebytes put on an encouraging performance. Browser Guard has expanded its coverage in several ways since my last review. For one, it marks up search results with red, green, or gray icons to indicate dangerous, safe, or unknown links. Browser Guard also automatically rejects those annoying cookie permission pop-ups and GDPR-specific pop-ups. Several other advanced features, including website access control and setting import/export, are reserved for paying customers. I also put Browser Guard through my standard phishing protection test. Phishing sites don’t try to infect your computer with malware. Rather, they masquerade as popular, secure sites, hoping to entice you to log in. If you do, you’ve given the fraudsters your login credentials. Whatever the account was, whether for online banking, dating, email, or some other purpose, the creators of the phishing page own it now. For this test, I scrape hundreds of recently reported fraudulent URLs from pages that collect and analyze such things. I make sure to include both verified phishing pages and pages that haven’t yet been analyzed and blocklisted. I use a hand-coded tool to launch each URL simultaneously in four browsers, one protected by the antivirus under test and the other three by the built-in protection of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. The testing tool also lets me record how each browser handles the URL. Keep in mind that every time I run this test, I use a different set of test URLs, but they're always the freshest ones available. If any of the four browsers don’t load a page, I discard it. If an alleged phishing page doesn’t truly fit the profile, meaning it doesn’t try to steal login credentials, I discard it. After processing all the URLs, I calculate the scores. Malwarebytes treated the phishing pages in much the same way it did malware-hosting pages, offering various reasons for blocking access, including phishing, riskware, and reputation. Malwarebytes scored 100% on this test, making it one of a dozen antivirus apps to achieve a perfect score. Among others in the winners’ circle are Avast, AVG, ESET NOD32 Antivirus, Guardio, and Surfshark One. Browser Guard also provides protection against fraudulent and malicious websites on the Mac. I tested Malwarebytes Premium Security for Mac with this same set of samples at the same time and found that it performed identically. New since my last review, all products in the Malwarebytes line include a page for identity protection. Those who purchase the top-tier Ultimate edition get full-on identity theft protection and remediation. The other apps, including the free one reviewed here, just get a digital footprint scan that reveals whether your email has appeared in a data breach. You can run the scan on as many emails as you like. However, in each case, you must prove your ownership of the address by supplying an emailed confirmation code. By observation, using this feature also opts you in to receive regular emails from Malwarebytes. After a quick scan, Malwarebytes summarizes its results with the number of exposures in five categories: Data breaches, SSN, Passwords, Personal Information, and Accounts. Clicking any of these lists provides details about the category. By default, it masks portions of the exposed data, but you can reveal those if you wish. For data breaches, you can dig one level deeper. At this point, Malwarebytes offers details about the breach itself and lists the specific elements of your private data that were exposed. Clicking the button titled Protect your identity simply takes you online to purchase the full identity protection service. The same happens if you click the Take Action button on the main report page. It’s worth noting that the digital footprint feature in the Mac edition works completely differently. The scan launches in your browser, and the report is awkward by comparison. At the time of my previous review, my Malwarebytes contacts said that the Mac edition was slated to move the digital footprint into the app, as it is on Windows. Apparently, that hasn’t happened yet. Clicking the Tools icon from the main window’s left-side menu brings up a page of—you guessed it—tools. The page is divided into four sections: Windows Firewall Control, System Tweaks, Startup Applications, and File Shredder. There’s not much meat to the startup control system. It lets you reversibly disable apps and components that launch at startup, something you can do just as easily using Task Manager. Norton’s startup manager, by contrast, lists resource usage and prevalence for each app launched at startup, and offers you the option to simply delay launch rather than disable it. As for controlling Windows Firewall, I will grant that the firewall’s own user interface leaves a lot to be desired. Malwarebytes makes the current settings clear and lets you easily make changes. But how many users have even the slightest urge to configure Windows Firewall? When you delete a file in Windows, it’s not really gone. Rather, it goes to the Recycle Bin, from which you can recover it if deletion was a mistake. Even if you bypass the Recycle Bin or empty it, the file’s data remains on disk, with a marker indicating it can be used for storage as needed. You can recover recently deleted files using third-party utilities or the Windows File Recovery Tool. That’s awkward when you need to truly and permanently delete a sensitive file. The file shredder tool handles this problem by overwriting each file’s data before deleting it. By default, it runs a single overwrite pass with random data. That’s enough to foil software-based forensic recovery. If your files are so sensitive that you worry the feds (or the mob) might attempt hardware-based recovery, you can crank the shredding mode up to Thorough or Paranoid…but only if you upgrade to the paid version of Malwarebytes. That leaves the system tweaks, by far the largest part of the tools collection. When you first open the tweaks page, you see a warning that this section contains experimental features and a recommendation to back up your system before using them. The tweaks are divided into four groups: Tools, Privacy, Gaming, and Miscellaneous. Note that you only get the full range of tools if you’re running Windows 11. In particular, Windows 10 users don’t get access to the tweaks page. There’s nothing here that you couldn’t accomplish by delving into Settings or Control Panel, but the Malwarebytes developers have curated their own collection of tools they think you might find useful. When you select the Tools sub-page, you can perform various resets, run a system integrity check, or launch the built-in disk cleanup tool. The handful of Gaming tweaks may marginally improve your experience. Not surprisingly, the Miscellaneous tweaks are a mixed bag. You can easily show file extensions or show hidden files, and dark mode is just a click away. If you dislike the Windows 11 two-tier context menu for files, you can flip back to the Windows 10 style. There’s a toggle to put the kibosh on Copilot. And so on. When I last reviewed this app, Privacy was just a sub-page of Tools, with a handful of toggles, mostly related to ads, within Windows. The new Privacy Controls page does much more. This page has three tabs: Windows Privacy settings, Remote Desktop programs, and Webcam Monitoring. The first tab expands on the ad and privacy data settings from the previous version. On the Remote Desktop management page, you see a list of programs that can connect to your device for remote control. Malwarebytes alerts you when it discovers such a program. For trusted apps, you can turn off the alert. My test virtual machine doesn’t have a (virtual) webcam, so I can’t test the Webcam Monitoring feature. It “lists apps that access your webcam so you can review and manage them.” As with most similar features, it alerts you when it detects a program attempting to access the webcam, giving you the option to mark the program as trusted or, if it’s unfamiliar, block and uninstall it. Since my last review, this app now incorporates scam detection technology. Just click the Scam Guard icon in the left-side menu to start a conversation. You can ask security questions, drop in suspected links for analysis, paste in dubious messages, and more. This feature is effectively an AI chatbot devoted to security and scams. You can discuss its responses, ask for more details, or just keep the conversation going. Note that even if you don’t have Malwarebytes installed, you can get some degree of help with scams using the online scam checker. Just visit the site and enter a suspicious link, or check a phone number to see if it’s been implicated in scams. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Malwarebytes Free is a useful tool. If you carry a thumb drive full of security tools, it's worth including. But remember, it offers no real-time protection, so it can't help you with ransomware. And based on our tests, it may not remove every trace of detected malware infestations. Use it along with Avast One Free or AVG AntiVirus Free (both Editors’ Choice winners for free antivirus) or another antivirus that provides real-time protection. item.title: REVIEW: Roborock Saros 20 Flow Review: Hope You Like Spending Money
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Last month, Roborock released the Saros 20 Flow. It’s a hideously expensive $1,700 robot vacuum that comes with boastful claims about its powerful suction, slim build, and self-maintaining features. And if everything about that appears to describe every other high-end robot vacuum you’ve read about lately, that’s because it often does. The Saros 20 Flow is a redux of the Saros 20 with one key improvement: it uses a roller mop instead of a pair of spinning pads. In my experience, roller mops are just better at handling stuck-on crud and heavier liquid messes, and that’s proven true during my testing of the 20 Flow over the last week. That comes with a bit of a compromise, as the 20 Flow stands 3.5 inches tall, compared to its predecessor’s 3.13 inches. It’s about three-quarters of an inch taller if you factor in its LiDAR sensor disc, though that lowers into its body as needed to fit under short furniture. The two floor bots look noticeably different as a result of these changes but otherwise are nearly identical when you pull them up in Roborock’s specs comparison tool. In many areas, the Saros 20 Flow is one of the best robot vacuums I’ve used. It’s great at cleaning hair and dirt out of carpet, it mops with the best of them, it gets around without any major issues, and its dock is mercifully quiet when emptying the robovac’s dustbin. It also supports local control via the Roborock app when the internet goes down. Nevertheless, I’m not convinced most people should bother siphoning off most of the cost of a 14-inch MacBook Pro from their bank accounts to own one. A great mopping, sweeping robovac that lacks many of the issues I have with the category, except for its price. It’s difficult to discern the Saros 20 Flow from some competing products, particularly the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra Roller, which has a nearly identical set of features, down to the roller mop and little robotic legs for boosting it over up to 1.77-inch transitions. The Aqua10 is a bit taller, at nearly four inches with its LiDAR disc retracted. And it only offers 30,000Pa suction, whereas the Saros 20 Flow matches its predecessor at 36,000Pa. (Don’t take those numbers too seriously—they’re among the highest you’ll find in a robovac, but even assuming both companies are measuring the same way, suction isn’t everything.) I had a nicer time setting up the Saros 20 Flow than I’ve had with many of its peers, which often come with a ton of trash to throw away, like foam inserts in crevices and plastic that you have to peel off the robot and the dock itself. The 20 Flow came with a bit of that—the robot and its dock were packed in bags and thick molded pulp, with a bit of tape holding the dock’s water tanks in place. But once I’d dealt with all that, I just plugged the dock in, snapped a little ramp onto the front, filled the water tanks, and slid the bot into its lower cavity. I then added the device to the Roborock app, which just involved holding down the home and power buttons on top of the robot to get it into pairing mode, tapping the “+” button in the upper right corner of the app’s home screen, scanning a QR code under a cover on top of the device, and entering my Wi-Fi information to get it on the network. Then the app prompted me to start mapping. I did this initial run—which took eight minutes for about 450 square feet—and most of my targeted testing at my partner’s house. After mapping, I performed the usual ritual of adjusting the map by dividing and combining and renaming rooms that the app tried to automatically separate and identify. I appreciate the effort, but the Roborock app was about as good as any other robovac software at this—which is to say, it only got about half of it right and otherwise did things like combining the hallway and bathroom into one big, weirdly shaped bathroom. In the Roborock app, the Saros 20 Flow follows most of the conventions of other robovac apps from Dreame, Ecovacs, and Anker. You start on a main screen with a map and controls that allow you to start a job and set the parameters of your clean. For example, you could instruct the device to vacuum two rooms but mop only one. As with most robot vacuums, there is no mop-only option. You can set the 20 Flow on your whole home, specify particular rooms or just custom portions of your home (i.e., “zones” that you define by drawing a rectangle on the map where you want it to work), or carry out routine cleanings you define in the app. Pop into the robot’s settings, and you’ll be able to tweak things like whether it cleans carpets in separate passes from hard floors, does it all at once, or ignores carpeted areas entirely. You can turn its sensor cluster on or off and control movements such as its swinging side brush and sliding mop roller. It uses AI for object detection, and you can turn that off as well. Local, internet-free control (for once) I was surprised to find that the Saros 20 Flow can be fully controlled (and its settings tweaked) using its app even when I disconnected my router from the internet. That’s very unusual and great if you’re security- or privacy-conscious and have the know-how to keep a device on your network but closed off from the wider internet. All of the other robovacs I’ve tested, apart from the Matic, require an active internet connection if you want to do anything at all in their dedicated apps. Shut off the internet, and the apps basically shrug and say they can’t find your robot. Some floor bots, such as the Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro and Eufy Omni E35, do support the universal smart home protocol Matter and can be connected to third-party platforms like Apple Home or Google Home. The Saros 20 Flow also has this support. In both theory and practice—for the bots I’ve tested in Apple Home, anyway—that means you can take advantage of local control through your smart home app when your internet is out, but you won’t be able to do much more than send the robot to clean specific rooms or return it to its dock, nor will you get notifications when said dock is out of clean water. That’s good enough for daily use, but Roborock still deserves some praise for enabling local control in its own app. Every robot vacuum maker should, and the vast majority simply do not. The Saros 20 Flow doesn’t suffer from many of the same issues that have plagued pricey robovacs I’ve tested in the past. It didn’t dump out dirt and dust when transitioning between floor types like the Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicyclone, nor poop out balled-up hair like the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra Roller, and I never found it inexplicably scouring one area for too long or repeatedly bumping the same spot on a wall the way the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete (I swear, these names) did. Rugs and hard flooring mostly looked meticulously swept and vacuumed (including in corners, where the Roborock’s side brush stretched out to sweep) where the Saros 20 Flow went, although it didn’t always pick up flat objects like scraps of paper. It also left floors spic and span where it mopped, and its mop even cleaned up part of a mysterious black stripe on a faux-wood laminate floor—perhaps a bit of shoe rubber rubbed off by a child?—that I’d purposefully avoided manually removing to see if any robot vacuums could actually deal with it. The 20 Flow likewise excelled at targeted tests. It got more dumped-out rice than any other vacuum I’ve run my usual rice-collecting test on. I only found five grains that it had flung away with its side brush and not managed to collect; the Omni E35 came in at 10 grains, while others I’ve tested have left too many to bother counting. And it did just as well as the Roomba Max 775, Matic, and Omni E35 at clearing ketchup I’d squirted on the floor, without leaving behind a sticky residue like every mop pad-equipped bot I’ve tested, or depositing the stuff elsewhere, as the Eufy Omni E28 did. The Saros 20 Flow is also pretty good at navigation and object avoidance, and it never got stuck or slammed into walls or furniture during testing, but it wasn’t without issues. It tended to roll over cables and either suck them up or drag them across the floor. And it had a hard time finding its dock in my partner’s house, where the only open space left it with just two to three feet of clearance. It always got there eventually but sometimes took as long as 12 minutes to figure out the right approach angle. In fairness, Roborock recommends leaving four feet of space in front of the dock, which is pretty standard for robot vacuums, but I tested it anyway, because not everyone has a room with such generous space. So far, only the Matic has handled that same spot without issue. Battery life and cleaning time were about on par with those of Roborock’s Qrevo 2 Pro, which I tested over the summer. The 20 Flow vacuumed then mopped my 750-square-foot apartment in just over two hours, ending the job with 48% of its battery remaining. The Qrevo 2 Pro did the same job in exactly two hours with 52% remaining. Other robots I’ve timed with the same conditions took longer: the Roomba Max 775 ended the job with 36% battery after about two-and-a-half hours, and the Narwal Freo Z10 Turbo took two hours and 49 minutes to finish with 40% battery. The Saros 20 Flow is a bit loud when it’s vacuuming, especially on carpets, where it boosts its suction to compensate and is raucous enough that you’d have to raise your voice to talk over it. Most similar bots I’ve tested are quieter—sometimes very much so. The Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone, for instance, is so quiet that I sometimes found myself checking to make sure it was actually doing something when I tested it. The 20 Flow’s noise while mopping is about the same as that of other roller mop models I’ve tested, which is to say that you can hear its roller mop motor turning but can talk over it just fine. What does make up for the Roborock’s noise is how quiet its auto-emptying dock is compared to those of other robot vacuums. In fact, when emptying the 20 Flow’s dustbin, it’s among the quietest docks that I’ve ever tested, even quieter than that of the Omni E35. However, in an otherwise silent room, I found the fan that dries the Saros 20 Flow’s mop roller uncomfortable to listen to after a while, though I didn’t realize that until the fan stopped and sudden relief washed over me. I’m not sure why I disliked the noise so much; maybe it was just humming at a frequency my ears aren’t used to. Thankfully, you can tweak how noisy it is by switching on “Eco” drying mode in the dock’s settings menu. Eco drying takes longer and isn’t ideal in a humid environment, but it’s nearly inaudible. I had only one truly big annoyance with the Saros 20 Flow’s cleaning abilities. As with most other robot vacuums, you can send Roborock’s device to clean specific areas of a room that you define by drawing a rectangle on the app’s map. But for some reason, the Saros just refused to vacuum rugs in this mode. It would sweep and mop hard floors within the zone but ignore carpeted areas, and when I drew the rectangle entirely inside of a rug, it would leave its dock, announce “cleaning path abnormal” from its speaker, and re-dock. I asked Roborock about this behavior and will update this review when it responds. Great robovac, but who cares when it’s $1,700? The Roborock Saros 20 Flow is just about as good as multifunction sweeping and mopping disc-shaped robovacs get. It did an excellent job pulling dirt, hair, and dust out of my carpets, never tried to eat clothing, and didn’t smack into any furniture or walls. And despite not having manually defined carpeted areas, I never caught it mopping my rugs. Like the Saros 20 it follows, it’s a great all-around floor bot. The 20 Flow isn’t perfect, though. There was that whole thing where it wouldn’t touch carpets inside custom zones. It’s also fairly noisy when vacuuming, which I’m willing to forgive given its overall good performance, but it might bother folks who are especially sensitive to sound. Those issues are small potatoes compared to the problems I’ve experienced with most other similar robot vacuums, though. The real problem is that $1,700 price tag. Look, I like the idea of not having to mop or vacuum my own floors as much as the next person, but you can get something this good for a lot less money elsewhere. Roborock’s own Qrevo 2 Pro, for example, does nearly as well in almost every way, except for object avoidance—the 2 Pro isn’t designed for small objects like cables and such, so it will eat them—for nearly $1,000 less. I’d rather tidy up a little before a clean, thank you. But even if you don’t mind spending that kind of money, you’ll get better object avoidance from the $1,300 Eufy Omni E35 or the $1,500 Matic. Those have their own trade-offs, of course—the Omni E35 is about an inch taller and still bumped walls and furniture regularly when I tested it, and the Matic’s boxy, seven-inch-high form factor excludes it from cleaning under things like beds and couches. Of course, all of that costs a lot more money than your average stick vacuum and a Swiffer, but hey, some folks have money to burn, and it is nice not to have to clean your floors yourself.

item.title: REVIEW: De’Longhi All-In-One review: one clever brewer for drip, espresso, and cold brew
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine brews your coffee your way: espresso, drip coffee, cold brew, and iced coffee. Plus, a built-in frother whisk and a steam wand for milk expand the its repertoire to just about any sort of coffee beverage. Brew a single shot of espresso, a whole carafe of drip coffee, or any size in between. - +Makes six drip coffee sizes ranging from 8oz to a 60oz carafe - +Built-in frother whisk and a steam wand for milk - +Has auto-start function and keep-warm plate Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: two-minute review The De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine brews every sort of coffee beverage you can think of. Granted, it's not fully automatic, so you'll have to be the barista, but getting started is easy and you'll be able to make a wide variety of drinks with very little practice. Make drip coffee the traditional way, by measuring out coffee grounds into the basket. A reusable plastic filter is included, but you can use a cone #4 paper filter if you prefer. The large carafe makes 60 ounces of coffee, and the half-carafe setting brews 30 ounces. You can pre-set the machine to automatically begin brewing at a certain time. The warming plate will keep your coffee hot or reheat it. A pull-down tray holds your mug so you can brew a single serving of coffee right into it. Choose the 8oz, 12oz, 16oz, or 20oz mug/travel mug setting. There are Classic and a Bold settings for drip coffee, so you can adjust the flavor to suit your preferences. The espresso portafilter comes with two filter baskets, one for brewing a single espresso and one for a double espresso. The machine uses 15 bars of pressure to make espresso. The adjustable steam wand has a Latte setting, which heats your milk without scalding it, and a Cappuccino setting, which steams and foams your milk of choice. This wand also dispenses fresh hot water for Americanos or non-coffee drinks. There is a frother whisk tucked into the side of the machine that just froths your milk, which is perfect for cold foam (or hot foam if you pre-heat your milk). As with any coffee machine, you'll need to clean everything after you're done brewing. Many of the parts can go into the dishwasher, and the parts that do need to be hand-washed are quick and easy to clean. De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: price and availability - Available for purchase in the US on DeLonghi's website, Target, Best Buy, Amazon, and more - Retails for $349.95 (roughly £260 / AU$520) The De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine is available at many retails online and in brick-and-mortar stores, such as DeLonghi's website, Target, Amazon, and many more. The retail price is $349.95, but it's frequently sold all over for under $300. That works out at approximately £260 / AU$520, but the machine is currently only available in the US. It comes in just one colorway, the black and silver shown here. De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: specs De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: design The De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine is cleverly designed to brew just about any sort of coffee beverage you might like, from a single espresso to a full carafe of drip coffee. A built-in steam wand and a frothing whisk whip up your milk your way. While it's not an automatic machine, it's easy to use and easy to clean up afterwards. During setup, you can use the touchscreen control panel to set the altitude at which you're using the machine (water boils at a lower temperature at high altitudes, which can result in coffee being under-extracted. You can also adjust the beep tone, water hardness, keep-warm temperature/time, and the hours format. The De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine comes with all of the accessories you need. It comes with a reusable plastic filter for drip coffee, though you can use a paper cone #4 filter if you like. The included two-sided drip coffee measuring scoop also acts a clip for your coffee bag. There's also a lever that allows you to pause brewing partway through; switch it from 'Coffee' to 'Stop' to halt the flow. The portafilter for making espresso comes with two filter baskets. The smaller filter basket makes a single espresso and the larger one makes a double. The metal lid on the top of the machine opens to a compartment for storing the espresso filter baskets when not in use. A double-ended scoop/tamper is included for precise measuring and tamping of grounds. There are two different options for preparing the milk you want to add to your coffee or espresso. The frother whisk (which is just like that of the Ninja Prestige DualBrew System) tucks into the side and pulls out when you need it. This simply froths your milk; it doesn't heat the milk. The steam wand on the front of the machine has two different settings. The Latte setting steam heats your milk while the Cappuccino setting steam heats and foams your milk at the same time. You can also dispense fresh hot water from the steam wand to make non-coffee beverages or add a little hot water to your espresso for an Americano. Both the whisk and the wand can be easily removed and hand-washed. The carafe rests on a heated plate, which will keep your coffee hot or reheat it for up to four hours. But if you're brewing a smaller portion directly into a mug, remove the carafe pull down the small platform from the machine. On the espresso side, the espresso drip tray can be moved up and down to accommodate the size of cup or mug you're using. The De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine is well designed to make all of your favorite coffee and espresso beverages. While it's not a tiny machine, it's not that large considering all of the features that it packs in. De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: performance - Makes countless amazing coffee and espresso beverages I brewed many different styles of coffee beverages. It's hard to imagine a type of drink that you couldn't make quite easily with the De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine. I started by making a single eight-ounce cup of coffee. I pulled out the platform and set my mug upon it. I measured out the amount of coffee suggested in the user guide into the plastic reusable filter. I selected the 'bold' setting and started the brew. In just about three minutes, I had a hot cup of delicious coffee in my hand. Regular drip coffee — carafe with Auto On and Keep Warm functions The night before I wanted a pot of coffee, I set up the Auto-On function and measured out the appropriate amount of coffee for a half carafe. The Keep Warm function turns on automatically when you're using the carafe; the is no heater in the smaller mug platform. I woke up about an hour after my coffee was ready and found it still fresh and quite hot. You can adjust the time and temperature of the warming plate, but I just used the default. I brewed a single espresso with ease. I chose the smaller filter basket and inserted it into the portafilter. The user guide recommends running a warm-up cycle with just water so I did that first. Then I used the included measuring scoop and put the grounds into the filter basket. The other end of the measuring scoop is a tamper, so I used that to tamp down my grounds. Brewing time was less than a minute. The espresso was very strong and had a generous crema. I made an espresso as directed. As the user guide suggested, I started with 3.5 ounces of milk in a container that can hold a lot more than that. I used a full-fat oat milk. I set the steam wand to the Cappuccino setting and started frothing. It frothed up to about 12 ounces, so it more than tripled in volume. The froth had big bubbles which were quite sturdy and held up well to stirring. This was quite tasty. A latte is similar to a cappuccino, only instead of added steamed milk plus lots of froth, you just add steamed milk. At least, that's a latte according to the user guide. Of course you can adjust the recipes as you like. Again, I made an espresso and poured 3.5 ounces of oat milk into a measuring cup. This time, I set the steam wand on the Latte setting. The milk did more than double in volume due to the steam, but there was almost no foam. I poured what I wanted into the espresso and it was delicious. In general coffee terms, a cold brew is brewed in the refrigerator for eight or more hours for a strong but smooth brew. Technically, a coffee machine can't make cold brew like that, but it does have a Cold Brew setting so I tested that out. I set up the coffee using a paper filter as recommended in the user guide. Brewing was slow, it took about 12 minutes to brew eight ounces of lukewarm coffee. This wasn't my favorite setting to be honest. Once I added ice, the coffee went pretty weak. This special setting brews a small amount of coffee very strongly, intended to be brewed over ice. I measured the recommended amount of coffee into the reusable coffee filter. I put a container half-filled with ice on the coffee platform, as the user guide suggested. I used the eight-ounce Over Ice setting and it took only three minutes to brew. This is a quarter of the time it took to brew the same size serving of cold brew. I preferred this method for making iced coffee, it tasted better to my palette. The coffee strength held up better to the ice using this setting. The frother whisk is different from the steam wand. It foams but doesn't add any steam to your milk. It also doesn't change the temperature. So, it's perfect if you want cold foam for your favorite iced coffee beverage. It can also make hot foam, you just have to heat your milk before using this. I decided to make an iced coffee with cold foam using some of the iced coffee I had made previously. I put a few ounces of oat milk into a small glass jar and frothed it. It quickly tripled or quadrupled in volume, though for some reason it wasn't as airy-looking as my steamed foam was. I poured what I wanted into my mug. The foam held up well to stirring. Should you buy the De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine? The De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine makes real espresso (and double espresso) with 15 bars of pressure and six different serving sizes of real drip coffee. You can even set up the machine to make your coffee the next morning and keep it warm for you. The De’Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine makes iced coffee two different ways. With both a Cold Brew setting and an Over Ice setting, you're sure to find a method you like. This machine offers several different ways to froth milk. The built-in frother whisk makes cold foam (or hot foam if you pre-heat your milk) and tucks away when not in use. The steam wand has two different settings, Cappuccino for steamed and foamed milk, Latte for just steamed. If you're not going to use most of the features, it's not going to be worth the space or the expense to buy this machine. Of course you can buy whole beans, but you'll have to grind them yourself before using them. This machine only takes pre-ground coffee beans. While this machine lets you make just about anything, you still have to do the work of measuring the coffee into the filter and dumping out the used grounds and cleaning the filter after each use. De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: also consider Ninja AutoBarista Pro Fully Automatic Espresso Machine If you do want to make your drinks with just the touch of a button, you'll want a fully automatic machine like this one. You just add water and whole beans once or twice a week and the machine does most of the work. If you don't really need espresso but you do want most of the other features, consider the Braun OptiBrew Pro for about $100 less. It does do a concentrated coffee shot which is similar to espresso and might do the trick for you. How I tested the De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine I brewed and drank quite a bit of coffee. On the coffee side of the machine, I brewed a single serving cup, a half carafe (using the Auto-On and Keep Warm features), a Cold Brew, and an Over Ice coffee. I frothed some oat milk using the frother whisk and added that to some of the iced coffee. On the espresso side, I made an espresso, a cappuccino, and a latte. I also used the hot water feature and made some herbal tea. After each brew, I cleaned all of the parts either by hand or in the dishwasher. item.title: REVIEW: Cockpit-Simulator 737X CDU (v2) Review: An Essential Component for Flight Sim Enthusiasts
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The CS 737X CDU (v2) brings an authentic, premium-build Boeing 737 Control Display Unit to the home cockpit, but its high price makes it a niche product for serious flight sim enthusiasts. - +Accurate 1:1 replica of the real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits. Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment. Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024. The Real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality. The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot. The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys. Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell. The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator. The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck. The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch. The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup. The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button. For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes: - 45 minutes from Las Vegas, Nevada to Ontario, California - 2 hours from Phoenix, Arizona to San Francisco, California - 5 hours from Oakland, California to Honolulu, Hawaii This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration. For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site. Our flow was similar in each case: - Import the payload & fuel for the flight - Select the instrument departure and planned approach - Import the performance numbers on the PERF INIT page - Complete the takeoff performance pages - Complete the APPROACH REF page as we get closer to the approach phase The overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive. This is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display. One of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized. We were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight plans loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator. The CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup. This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

item.title: SALES: The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones, bird feeders, health trackers, slushy machines, AI mattress pads, you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive, but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves. If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season. We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader. Xteink X3 ($55) – a budget pick for someone techy It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running. XTeink X4 Pro ($99) – it has a backlight! If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro. It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone. Boox Palma Pro 2 ($400) – a phone-sized e-reader without the drawbacks If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not. If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour, which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out! Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not? Ember Mug 3 ($99) – for the tea lover who’s really particular The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying! This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for! Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer ($449.99) – two appliances in one! Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances. GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro ($499.99) – if your fridge has a built-in ice maker, you just won’t understand Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you. What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones… Open AI Codex Micro ($230) – for the Codex evangelist When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro. Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware. Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years. For the person who’s desperate to log off As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life. Brick ($59) or Brick Night ($129) — a not-so-subtle gift for your friend who doomscrolls every night before bed For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs. It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I? Dumb Phone ($20 + service plan) – for someone who wants to try something new but can’t totally give up their iPhone I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone, Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!
