item.title: SALES: Best Christmas carols in London for 2026, from candlelit concerts to fun singalongs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Is there anything that says Christmas more than carols sung in centuries-old churches or on cobbled streets surrounded by twinkling lights? There are few things that make the city feel quite as magical as the festive season, and the best Christmas carols in London are certainly part of the magic. Christmas markets, ice-skating rinks and beautifully decorated hotels all have their charm, but there's something particularly special about gathering together to sing a few Christmas classics. Whether it's the sound of a live choir filling one of London's magnificent cathedrals, an intimate candlelit concert in a historic church or a cheerful round of carol-singing beneath the Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square, there's no shortage of ways to enjoy festive music in the city. And the good news is that you don't necessarily need to spend a fortune, with several free carol services taking place throughout December. From grand musical performances at the Royal Albert Hall to traditional carols accompanied by mince pies, here's where to enjoy Christmas carols in London in 2026. Where can I see Christmas carols in London? Some of the best places to see Christmas carols in London include the Royal Albert Hall, St Paul's Cathedral, Westminster Abbey, All Souls Langham Place and St Martin-in-the-Fields. For free performances, try Trafalgar Square or one of the city's traditional church carol services. Those looking for a candlelight concert can head to Union Chapel or Cadogan Hall. Will there be Christmas carols at the Royal Albert Hall in 2026? Yes, the Royal Albert Hall will host its annual Christmas carol concerts from 19 to 24 December 2026. The performances feature live orchestras, choirs and audience singalongs, with a programme of traditional Christmas carols and festive favourites. Tickets are available through the venue's official website. What time are Christmas carols at Trafalgar Square? Christmas carol performances at Trafalgar Square take place throughout December, with individual choirs allocated approximately one-hour sessions. Performances have traditionally taken place in the late afternoon and evening, but there is no fixed schedule. Remember that, if you wish, you can also apply to sing! Where can I find Christmas carol concerts in London in 2026? Christmas carol concerts take place across London throughout December, from grand performances at the Royal Albert Hall and Cadogan Hall to traditional services at St Paul's Cathedral, Westminster Abbey and Southwark Cathedral. Many require advance booking, particularly the larger concerts, while churches such as All Souls Langham Place offer free services. For the best availability, it's worth booking popular events well ahead of Christmas. Few Christmas traditions are quite as spectacular as an evening of carols at the Royal Albert Hall. The Kensington landmark is hosting 15 festive concerts in the days leading up to Christmas, bringing together the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, National Youth Choir, Royal Choral Society and British Imperial Military Band for a series of musical performances. Expect a mixture of traditional carols, Christmas classics and plenty of opportunities to sing along, whether you're a confident singer or someone who usually prefers to listen – there's something rather special about hearing thousands of voices joining together in one of London's most beautiful concert halls. Address: Royal Albert Hall, Kensington Gore, London SW7 2AP 2. Christmas Carol Services at St Paul's Cathedral Being able to do incredible things like listening to Christmas carols inside St Paul's Cathedral, with its magnificent dome and centuries of history, is what makes London one of the best cities to visit in December. The cathedral's annual programme of Advent and Christmas services includes traditional carol services on 23 and 24 December, with performances by the St Paul's Cathedral Choir and readings retelling the nativity story. Families can also attend a dedicated service on 19 December, while classical music lovers should look out for Handel's Messiah on 2 and 10 December. And for those who prefer to celebrate Christmas as the clock strikes midnight, the cathedral also holds a Midnight Eucharist service on Christmas Eve, beginning at 11pm. Date: 23–24 December 2026, 4pm; additional Christmas events throughout December Address: St Paul's Churchyard, London EC4M 8AD Price: Free, but tickets are required for the Christmas Carol Services Christmas in London can be expensive, but luckily, not everything comes with a price tag. Just a short walk from the shopping crowds of Oxford Circus, All Souls Langham Place is hosting 24 free carol services throughout December. A live choir and orchestra perform traditional carols and festive favourites, while readings retell the nativity story. There are plenty of opportunities to join in, too, and afterwards, visitors can enjoy complimentary mince pies and hot Christmas punch. The services are so popular that the church even sets up a large screen outside for those who can't find a seat inside, so make sure to arrive early. Date: 12, 13, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22 and 23 December 2026, at 3.30pm, 5.30pm and 7.30pm Address: All Souls Church, 2 All Souls Place, London W1B 3DA 4. Carols by Candlelight at St Martin-in-the-Fields Just a stone's throw from Trafalgar Square, St Martin-in-the-Fields is a lovely place to escape the busy streets of central London for an hour or two. The 18th-century church hosts a busy programme of Christmas concerts throughout December, from traditional carols to classical performances by candlelight. Depending on the concert, you can expect choral music, familiar festive favourites and the chance to join in with a few Christmas classics. Families can also book one of the shorter Festive Family Carols performances, including a concert on 19 December. Afterwards, head outside to admire the towering Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square, a gift from Norway that has become one of London's best-known festive traditions. Date: Selected dates throughout December 2026; Festive Family Carols on 19 December at 1pm Address: St Martin-in-the-Fields, Trafalgar Square, London WC2N 4JJ Price: Varies by concert; Carols by Candlelit from £10 Not every Christmas carol concert in London requires a ticket or even a seat. Throughout December, choirs gather beneath the famous Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square to perform traditional carols, with some raising money for charity along the way. The towering Norwegian spruce has been gifted to London every year since 1947 as a symbol of gratitude for Britain's support during the Second World War, and is decorated with vertical strings of lights in the Norwegian tradition. Performances take place without a stage or PA system, giving the carol-singing a charmingly old-fashioned feel. Wrap up warmly, grab something hot to drink and enjoy a few Christmas classics right in the heart of London. Date: Throughout December 2026; individual choir dates and times to be announced Address: Trafalgar Square, London WC2N 5DN 6. Christmas with the Choir of Westminster Abbey With more than a thousand years of history behind its walls, Westminster Abbey is a rather special place to enjoy Christmas music. On 19 December, the Abbey's renowned choir will perform a festive concert featuring traditional carols, seasonal readings and Benjamin Britten's A Ceremony of Carols, performed by the young choristers accompanied by a harp. Conducted by Andrew Nethsingha, the programme takes inspiration from the traditional Festival of Lessons and Carols, bringing together familiar Christmas music and choral works in one of London's most historic settings. The concert lasts around 80 minutes, leaving plenty of time to enjoy the Christmas lights around Westminster afterwards. Address: Westminster Abbey, 20 Dean's Yard, London SW1P 3PA Price: From £17.28 including booking fee 7. Carols by Candlelight at the Tower of London Spending an evening listening to Christmas carols inside the Tower of London isn't something you get to do every day. On 10 December, the historic fortress opens its doors for a candlelit concert in the Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula, a Tudor church tucked within its walls. The Choir of the Chapel Royal will perform a selection of festive music and readings, including a new piece specially composed for the occasion by Becky McGlade. With the chapel illuminated by candlelight and the Tower's centuries of history all around you, it's certainly a memorable way to celebrate the festive season. Date: 10 December 2026, 7–8pm (arrive at the West Gate from 6.30pm) Address: Tower of London, London EC3N 4AB 8. Carols at Cadogan with The Bach Choir If you love a good Christmas singalong, this one's for you. On 15 December, The Bach Choir takes over Cadogan Hall for an evening of traditional carols and newer festive compositions, accompanied by London City Brass, organ and percussion. With around 100 singers on stage, conducted by David Hill, expect plenty of opportunities to join in with familiar Christmas favourites. The programme also includes the winning entry from the annual Sir David Willcocks Carol Competition, which gives composers of all ages the chance to have their work performed. The concert lasts approximately two hours, including an interval, so there's plenty of time to get into the Christmas spirit. Address: Cadogan Hall, 5 Sloane Terrace, London SW1X 9DQ Price: From £20, plus £4.50 transaction fee per online booking 9. A Christmas Celebration at Westminster Cathedral If you love choral music, Westminster Cathedral's annual A Christmas Celebration is well worth adding to your December plans. Taking place over two evenings, the concert brings together the Westminster Cathedral Choir and Orchestra, conducted by Simon Johnson, for a programme of Christmas music and readings reflecting on the birth of Christ. Celebrity readers will also take part, although their names have yet to be announced. The cathedral itself is worth a visit, with its red-brick exterior, Byzantine-inspired architecture and elaborate mosaics offering a striking contrast to London's Gothic churches. Tickets also help support the work of the cathedral, making this a festive evening with a good cause behind it. Date: 16 and 17 December 2026, 7.30-9pm (doors open at 6.45pm) Address: Westminster Cathedral, Victoria Street, London SW1P 1LT

item.title: SALES: The best UK destinations for a literary-inspired romantic getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
With temperatures dropping, days getting shorter and the Christmas holidays just around the corner, there is no better time to think about a cosy winter getaway – preferably one that feels like stepping into the pages of your favourite fictional love story. Even the least romantic souls among us have been swept off their feet by 2026 romantic releases like Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility and Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights – and things are about to get even more dreamy with Jack Lowden as Mr Darcy in the new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton, coming to Netflix in December. And for those who prefer their love stories with a little magic, there's always romantasy, where witches, vampires and forbidden romances are all part of the appeal. But why settle for watching these romantic stories unfold on screen or reading about them when you could experience a little of that magic yourself? From the dramatic Cornish coastline that inspired Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca to the grand country estates of Jane Austen's novels and the historic libraries of Oxford, where the supernatural romance of A Discovery of Witches begins, Britain is full of places that look like they've been lifted straight from the pages of a romance or fantasy novel. Whether you're a fan of Austen's slow-burning love stories, gothic romance or the magical worlds of modern romantasy, these literary-inspired escapes offer the chance to follow in the footsteps of your favourite fictional characters – with a beautiful hotel to retreat to at the end of the day. The most romantic literary-inspired escapes to book in the UK Few love stories are quite as passionate or tragic as Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights. Set against the wild Yorkshire moors, the novel follows the tumultuous relationship between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff, whose love for one another turns into obsession and heartbreak. For a taste of Brontë's world, head to Haworth, where the author lived and wrote her only novel. Visit the Brontë Parsonage Museum before walking across the windswept moors that inspired her writing. Where to stay: Around 20 minutes away by car, Holdsworth House is a romantic 17th-century Jacobean manor surrounded by three acres of gardens, with individually decorated bedrooms, oak-panelled interiors and a restaurant serving seasonal dishes. No other literary couples are quite as beloved as Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy, whose complicated romance is at the heart of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice. Much of their story unfolds in the English countryside, but it's Derbyshire that offers one of the strongest connections to the novel. Here, you'll find Chatsworth House, the magnificent stately home long believed to have inspired Darcy's fictional estate of Pemberley. The house also famously stood in for Pemberley in the 2005 film adaptation starring Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen. Spend the day exploring its grand interiors and gardens before wandering through the surrounding Peak District countryside. Where to stay: Set on the Chatsworth Estate, just a 20-minute walk from the house, The Cavendish Hotel is an elegant country retreat with 28 bedrooms featuring antique furnishings and views over the surrounding parkland. For a particularly romantic stay, book the Splendid Room, which comes with a four-poster bed and marble-surround bath, before enjoying dinner at the hotel's Gallery Restaurant. For anyone who believes in second chances at love, Jane Austen's Persuasion is the perfect romantic read. The novel follows Anne Elliot and Captain Frederick Wentworth, who find themselves reunited eight years after their broken engagement. Much of the story unfolds in Bath, where Austen herself lived for several years. Follow in the footsteps of the two lovers with a stroll along Gravel Walk, the historic pathway where they finally open their hearts to one another, before exploring the city's elegant Georgian streets and stopping for afternoon tea at the Pump Room. Where to stay: Overlooking Queen Square in the heart of Bath, The Francis Hotel occupies a row of Georgian townhouses, with 98 beautifully appointed bedrooms, some overlooking the square. After a day exploring Austen's Bath, settle in for dinner at the hotel's Emberwood restaurant or book a relaxing treatment at its spa. With its mysterious country house, dark secrets and troubled marriage, Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca is one of the great gothic romances. The novel follows a young woman who marries the wealthy widower Maxim de Winter, only to find herself living in the shadow of his first wife, Rebecca. The Cornish coast plays a central role in the story, and du Maurier drew inspiration for the fictional Manderley from Menabilly, a secluded estate near Fowey where she later lived for many years. Follow in the author's footsteps with a walk along the South West Coast Path towards Polridmouth Cove, which also inspired a location in the novel. Where to stay: Overlooking the Fowey estuary, Fowey Hall is an elegant Victorian mansion with beautifully refurbished bedrooms. Spend the afternoon unwinding in the spa, complete with an indoor pool, steam room and hot tub, before settling in for dinner at the hotel's restaurant, which serves seasonal dishes made with locally sourced ingredients. Book: A Discovery of Witches – Deborah Harkness For a love story with a little magic, Deborah Harkness's A Discovery of Witches is hard to beat. Set partly in Oxford, the novel follows Diana Bishop, a historian and reluctant witch who discovers a mysterious enchanted manuscript in the Bodleian Library. Her discovery draws the attention of Matthew Clairmont, an enigmatic vampire, and sparks a forbidden romance that challenges the rules of their supernatural world. Follow in Diana's footsteps with a visit to the Bodleian Library before wandering through Oxford's historic colleges and atmospheric streets. Where to stay: Set on an 85-acre estate in the Oxfordshire countryside, Estelle Manor is a grand country-house hotel with 108 rooms, four restaurants and beautiful gardens. For a romantic afternoon, head to Eynsham Baths, the hotel's Roman-inspired spa, which features five pools, thermal facilities and couples' treatment suites. If you love a Regency romance with a touch of magic, Olivia Atwater's Half a Soul is one to add to your reading list. Set partly in a fantastical version of Regency London, the novel follows Theodora Ettings, a young woman cursed by a faerie who has stolen half her soul, leaving her without a sense of fear or embarrassment. When she meets Elias Wilder, the handsome but rather ill-mannered Lord Sorcier, an unlikely romance begins to blossom. For a taste of the world Atwater brings to life, explore London's elegant Georgian squares, wander through the streets of Mayfair and imagine the grand balls and high-society gatherings of the Regency era. Where to stay: Housed in a grand Edwardian building in Holborn, Rosewood London combines historic architecture with luxurious interiors and a beautiful courtyard. Spend the afternoon enjoying tea in the elegant Mirror Room before heading to Scarfes Bar for cocktails by the fire, or book a treatment at the hotel's Sense spa.

item.title: SALES: Where is hot in Europe in February? 12 dazzling spots that sizzle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
There’s something about a February holiday that feels especially appealing. After all, Christmas was ages ago by now, the excitement of the New Year has passed, and it’s pretty much cold, wet and miserable outside every day from now until May. And while you may think there are only two options: to go short haul and do a ski holiday or city break in Europe, or to jet off to the southern hemisphere for some winter sunshine, we shouldn’t forget that there are some corners of the continent that actually do reach the late teens and twenties this month. So, where are the warmest places in Europe in February? Unsurprisingly, the majority are located in southern Europe, in Spain and Portugal, with the perennially balmy Canary Islands being a go-to. But don’t sleep on the likes of Madeira, Cyprus, Sicily or Gibraltar, where you can also catch some decent rays. Without further ado, here’s where is hot in February in Europe. Where is hot in February and cheap? Spain and its Canary Islands are usually your best bet for a cheap and cheerful winter sun break in Europe in February. Both have well-established flight routes and tourism industries, which means that the options are endless, as opposed to some cities where only a handful of hotels are open and they can therefore charge a premium. Is Portugal warm in February? Parts of Portugal are warmer in February, but it is still very much winter here. That said, it’s always going to be balmier than in the UK, so if you don’t mind still wearing a light jacket and probably not sunbathing, then it’s fine for you. The capital city Lisbon boasts 16°C average highs, which cannot be sniffed at. Which part of Spain is warmest in February? Spain is lucky in that it boasts some of the hottest temperatures in Europe in February. Particular sun traps include Seville (18°C), Valencia (17°C), and Almería (18°C). Where is it warm in Italy in February? Southern Italy, or the ‘boot’, is the warmest part to visit in February. Think Calabria (15°C), the Amalfi Coast and Naples (14°C), and of course, the island of Sicily (15°C). Where is hot in Europe in February? Crete is Greece’s most southerly island, and as such, is also its warmest in the winter season. That said, it only reaches highs of around 16°C, and there’s still very much a chance of inclement weather, so it’s not really the time to be hitting the beach and it’s certainly a no-go for swimming in the sea. However, if you’re looking to experience the local culture and see the historical sites without the crowds (or the sweat), then this is an excellent time of year to do so. Just be aware that some hotels and restaurants will be closed for the off-season, so definitely do your research on where to stay and eat beforehand. Where to stay: Casa Delfino Hotel & Spa in Chania’s Old Town has a historic charm, with its Venetian-inspired architecture and famous black-and-white checkered courtyard. Family-run for six generations, it’s the perfect base from which to explore, with plenty of insider tips on what to do. Lisbon is one of our favourite European city breaks at any time of year, but it’s especially charming in February. That’s because without the blazing hot sun and crowds of tourists, you get to experience life here like a local. Temperatures are in the mid-teens, but the sun is shining, which means you’ll need a jacket and sunglasses in equal measure. It’s also much easier to walk the city at this time of year (and its famous hills), and there are virtually no queues for the likes of Jerónimos Monastery, Torre de Belém, and the historic neighbourhoods of Alfama and Baixa. Where to stay: The Ivens is our go-to year-round in Lisbon: this stylish five-star has one of the best locations in the Chiado neighbourhood, plus its restaurant Rocco is the place to see and be seen right now in the city. Madeira, despite being a Portuguese island, is actually closer to Africa than the Algarve, which goes some way to explaining why it’s one of the hottest places in Europe in February. This charming volcanic island has a lot to offer, but is particularly appealing to outdoorsy types who love a good hike, with trails through the mountains. Funchal, the capital, is where you’ll find the best restaurants and nightlife, not to mention its famous toboggan sledges, which will be far less busy in February too. Where to stay: The Savoy Palace is a wonderful all-rounder for couples and families, with extensive facilities including rooftop pool and kids club. The real draw here though, is the award-winning Laurea Spa, which has the distinction of being the biggest in Portugal – perfect after a long day hiking and tobogganing. Palermo might be at the lower end of the February temperatures listed here, with average highs of 15°C – but compared to the UK's frosty, rainy shores, it'll still feel like a balmy escape. Come summer, the Sicilian capital can become extraordinarily hot – so visiting in the off-season is a clever alternative. Spend days exploring the city's many bustling markets without the heaving crowds you can expect in peak season, and evenings drinking €2 Aperol Spritzes. Where to stay: Villa Igiea, a Rocco Forte Hotel, appeared on our Gold List in 2023, with Art Nouveau touches like grand frescoes and staircases. Spain's third-largest city is often still curiously overlooked by Brits – especially when you consider that the weather stays mild throughout the winter, offering up a short-haul sunshiny escape on a platter. There's a gorgeous Old Town, sleek rooftop bars for happy hour – plus the Mediterranean coast is within touching distance, if you're feeling confident enough to brave a bracing, cold-water dip. Where to stay: Hotel Palacio Vallier is set in a smart 19th-century townhouse, with 31 suites and rooms and a smart rooftop bar. While Europe isn’t short of destinations basking in mild temperatures, there’s no denying that fewer places warrant packing swimwear. The sun-soaked Canary Island of Tenerife, off the coast of West Africa, is one exception. There's plenty to do on the occasional overcast day, from the colourful Los Cristianos Street Market on Sundays to exploring the Parque Rural de Anaga nature reserve. For the most part, you’ll be baking on sandy swathes as the temperatures climb towards the mid-20s. Where to stay: The Ritz-Carlton Tenerife, Abama, is one of Europe’s most colourful stays. Take a dip in one of the countless swimming pools, break a sweat in the sprawling fitness and spa area, or listen to the crashing waves on the exclusive beach area. Seville is always a good idea – even more so when mild temperatures allow for sightseeing that won’t leave you soaked through. A long weekend is enough to top up the vitamin D reserves over long, sunny lunches, offering a chance to preview the spring and summer wardrobe. There are plenty of things to do across the city: soak up the sunshine on a bike ride through the parks, explore the Old Town on foot, or simply feast your way through one of Spain’s tastiest corners. Where to stay: For an affordable boutique stay with lashings of opulence – and super-snazzy interiors – look no further than Hotel Boutique Triana House. Cyprus is a favourite winter sun escape for a reason. It’s less crowded here than during the main holiday season, when it can feel slightly packed to the brim full of families, and there’s a slow, relaxed pace of expat life that feels particularly alluring. Paphos in particular has much going for it, including hikes along the Aphrodite Trail and through Paphos Forest, not to mention access to archaeological sites like the Tombs of the Kings. Be sure to head to the local markets and sample some in-season delicacies, such as Cypriot cake, coffee and of course, almonds. Where to stay: Almyra is a 187-room, family-run and family-friendly resort inspired by Aphrodite. Windows flood communal areas with natural light, while finishes of natural fabrics and Carrara marble create a calming space that’ll have you embracing the art of R&R immediately. People often forget about Malta, but it’s one of the real undiscovered gems of the Atlantic and well worth a visit. February is a lovely time of year to be here, as you can enjoy the variety of things the island has to offer without worrying about it being too hot and sticky. Spend a few days soaking up the foodie scene in the capital of Valletta first, before heading inland to the historic walled city of Mdina (major Game of Thrones vibes) and then island-hopping to Goza to see a totally different way of life. Where to stay: The Xara Palace is the only Relais & Châteaux property in Malta and makes for the chicest bolthole for a Maltese city break. It’s not unusual for temperatures to exceed 20°C, especially towards the end of the month. This offers winter sun-seekers the option of long beach days on wild stretches of sand, poolside sipping in sleek all-inclusive resorts or island exploration. In recent years, Lanzarote has remodelled itself as a hideout favoured by adrenaline junkies and sporty souls. Hike through the volcanic landscape, perfect your swing on the island’s golf courses, or take to the water for surfing, kitesurfing and sport fishing. Where to stay: For a Lanzarote bolthole with plenty of soul, check into the adults-only César Lanzarote Luxury Boutique Hotel. This independent, 20-room hotel’s spectacular cliff-top pool and terrace is particularly hard to leave. The Province of Almería is a dry, mountainous region in southern Spain, known for its wild coastline and charming resort towns. It’s long been a popular tourist spot in summer when families descend on beautiful beaches such as Playa de los Genoveses and Playa de Agua Amarga. Even if the temperature doesn’t warrant full immersion, the water’s warm enough for a paddle, and there’s no better way to spend long afternoons than with strolls through the hills and sands. Where to stay: With its clifftop infinity pool and numerous sprawling terraces, Villa Zambudio may claim the title of Almería’s fanciest rental. Yes, you’ll need a car to explore all this coastline offers, but it’s well worth it for the poolside days as the temperatures creep up. The first thing that strikes visitors arriving in Gibraltar is the similarity to the UK. As a British Overseas Territory, it’s a sunny version of the UK in many ways, and it can feel a little disorienting strolling past the likes of Hotel Chocolat and The Hummingbird Café, hand-held fan easing the baking temperatures. Gibraltar is often hot enough in February for al-fresco lunches and waterfront wandering – if the rain appears, just seek shelter in one of the local pubs. Where to stay: The Rock Hotel is often regarded as one of the best hotels in Gibraltar. The colonial-style hotel once hosted Sir Winston Churchill.

item.title: SALES: 10 Best Winter Hiking and Snowshoeing Pants
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
The best winter hiking and snowshoeing pants are highly breathable softshell pants that prevent perspiration from accumulating when hiking, snowshoeing, climbing/mountaineering, or even ski touring in winter. They’re made with woven nylon or polyester, which is warmer and more windproof than standard three-season hiking pants, and are treated with an exterior DWR coating to help repel water. Many softshell pants have features that can be used for multiple winter sports, while others are more hiking-specific. The fit also varies by activity: climbing-style pants tend to run slim, while hiking/snowshoeing pants are roomier and easier to layer. Popular features include a buried/integrated belt providing for hipbelt and climbing harness compatibility, zippered side vents, zippered pockets, and ankle adjustability. Be sure to read our FAQ below about how to choose the best softshell winter pants for your needs. Here are the 10 best softshell winter hiking and snowshoeing pants that we recommend. 4. Mountain Equipment Ibex and Chamois Pants 5. Fjallraven Abisko Winter Stretch Trousers 8. Outdoor Research Cirque III Softshell Pants What are the best winter hiking pants? Many experienced winter hikers prefer softshell winter pants because they’re simpler to use than wearing rain pants over a pair of long underwear. Softshell pants are also more form-fitting and don’t make any noise. The problem with rain pants and long underwear is that it can be difficult to vent your rain pants or take off your long underwear without first removing your rain pants and boots. Softshell pants are breathable enough, meaning that your sweat will evaporate through them if you start to warm up and perspire. Are softshell pants good for snow? Softshell pants are good for snow because they have a DWR coating on the exterior that repels water and they’re highly breathable so you don’t overheat. Hiking in snow or snowshoeing requires a lot of energy and it’s easy to overheat and perspire. You want to avoid getting too warm and sweating because it will wet your clothing and reduce its ability to insulate you. Are softshell pants waterproof? Softshell pants are far more breathable than the waterproof rain pants that some hikers wear, so you’ll stay cooler and perspire less when working hard when hiking up mountains or snowshoeing. While they have an external DWR repellent coating for enhanced rain resistance, they are not waterproof or as windproof as hard shell rain pants. We recommend carrying both softshell pants and rain pants on cold-weather hikes, the latter for rain and wind protection, as well as added warmth when layered over the softshell pants. Are softshell pants windproof? Softshell pants are more windproof and warmer than regular hiking pants, but they’re designed to be highly breathable and let some wind through. If you need protection from the wind, we’d recommend layering a pair of wind pants or rain pants over a pair of softshell pants when you need added wind protection. Should you wear a baselayer under softshell pants? You can wear a baselayer (long underwear) under softshell pants, but it’s often not necessary except on extremely cold days. Softshell pants are warmer than regular hiking pants and usually sufficient to keep you warm when you’re actively hiking or snowshoeing. If you need additional warmth because you’re being chilled by the wind or because you’re standing still and not moving and generating heat, you can warm up by wearing a pair of rain pants over your softshell pants. Also, if you wear a baselayer under softshell pants and find yourself overheating, it’s very difficult to delayer without taking off your boots and pants, unless your baselayer long underwear has side zips and is removable without requiring that you get undressed. How are softshell hiking pants different from ski pants? Ski pants are usually much heavier, bulkier, and warmer since there is so much start and stop activity involved especially if you’re skiing at a resort with chair lifts. many ski pants also have internal gaiters which are hot and awkward to use when hiking and snowshoeing. Why do softshell pants have a buried or integrated belt? A buried or integrated pants belt loops around your waist like a regular belt but is covered with fabric around the back and sides of the pant. This makes the belt compatible with a climbing harness or a backpack hipbelt. When climbing higher mountains, you may be required to rope-in with a climbing harness. Why do softshell pants have zippered pockets? Softshell pants have zippered pockets that are usually located in front of the pants and are positioned so they can be easily accessed even if you’re wearing a climbing harness. Zippered pockets are more streamlined than regular pockets and less likely to interfere with gear hanging from a climbing harness. Why do some softshell pants have ankle cuffs? Some softshell pants have a built-in ankle cuff on the inside of the legs to provide crampon protection when climbing, backcountry skiing, or winter hiking. The ankle cuff isn’t as substantial as a high gaiter and doesn’t replace wearing them, but can be a useful convenience for winter use, especially if you want to use the same pants for ski touring. Why do softshell pants have articulated knees? Articulated knees are baggier than the knees in regular pants and provide more freedom of movement especially for climbing. What are gusseted softshell pants? Gussetted pants have added fabric panels, usually triangular, that add more width to the crotch, making it easier to raise your knee when taking large steps or climbing vertical surfaces.
